title: Comparative Politics: Nature and Major Approaches

cards.b:
Comparative politics studies how political systems work by setting them side by side: states, regimes, parties, elections, institutions. It is the base of Paper II Section A, and it gives you tools you can use all over the optional.

The central question is simple: why do similar-looking countries end up different, and different ones alike? Why did India stay democratic after 1947 while most new states did not? Why do some economies become rich through state-led plans?

The syllabus asks for two things in this lesson: the nature of the field, and its major approaches. You need to know the comparative method, and a clear timeline of approaches: traditional, behavioural, structural-functional, political culture, political development, institutionalism and rational choice.

Examiners like thinkers with titles and years: Aristotle, Montesquieu, Almond, Easton, Lijphart, Sartori, Huntington, Skocpol. Add India as a case.

Comparative politics is the study of domestic politics across countries, using systematic comparison. International relations deals with relations between states; comparative politics asks about politics inside them.

Roy Macridis described the traditional field as "comparative government", which listed the formal institutions of countries one by one. The modern field asks causal questions, using concepts and evidence.

Aims

  • Describe political systems accurately.
  • Classify them: democracies, autocracies, presidential or parliamentary systems.
  • Explain outcomes: regime change, revolutions, party systems, welfare states.
  • Predict and test theories across cases.
  • Learn from others' experience (policy lessons).

Its roots are old. Aristotle's team studied the constitutions of 158 city-states (the Constitution of Athens survives). Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), linked laws to climate and society. Alexis de Tocqueville wrote Democracy in America (1835, 1840). James Bryce wrote Modern Democracies (1921).

Arend Lijphart, "Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method" (American Political Science Review, 1971), named four ways to test ideas: experimental, statistical, comparative and case study. The comparative method suits few cases but many variables. This is the "small N" problem.

J.S. Mill's System of Logic (1843) gave the logic. Adam Przeworski and Henry Teune, The Logic of Comparative Social Inquiry (1970), turned it into most similar and most different systems designs.

cards.h: Traditional approach and the behavioural revolution
cards.b:
Traditional (institutional-legal) approach. Before the 1940s, scholars described constitutions, legislatures and courts, mostly in Europe and the US. Herman Finer, Theory and Practice of Modern Government (1932), is an example. Criticisms: formal, descriptive, Eurocentric, silent on behaviour and society, and unscientific.

Behavioural revolution (1950s-60s). After the war, American political scientists turned to people's actual behaviour, with surveys and statistics. Their claims (David Easton): politics has regularities, theory should be tested, values and facts should be kept apart, and research should be systematic and use quantitative methods.

  • New states in Asia and Africa needed analysis. Old institutional tools did not fit them.
  • Gabriel Almond led a committee on comparative politics in the Social Science Research Council (1954).

Post-behaviouralism. Easton's 1969 American Political Science Association address, "The New Revolution in Political Science", argued for relevance and action: the field must tackle real problems, not just method.

David Easton, The Political System (1953) and A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965), saw politics as a system. Demands and support enter as inputs. The system converts them into decisions and policies (outputs). Feedback returns to the system.

Gabriel Almond, in "A Functional Approach to Comparative Politics" (in The Politics of Developing Areas, 1960), asked what functions every system must perform. G. Bingham Powell joined him in Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach (1966).

Almond's functions

Input: political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication.
Output: rule-making, rule application, rule adjudication.

A system is judged by its capabilities: extractive, regulative, distributive, symbolic and responsive. Strength: a common frame to compare all countries, including new ones. Weaknesses: conservative (bias toward stability), vague, and it takes a Western system as the model.

Political culture. Almond and Sidney Verba, The Civic Culture (1963), surveyed five countries (US, UK, West Germany, Italy, Mexico). They identified three types of orientation:

  • Parochial: little awareness of the national system.
  • Subject: aware, but passive.
  • Participant: active citizens.

A stable democracy needs a mix, the civic culture, with participation balanced by deference. Critics: circular logic, and it ignores power and inequality. Ronald Inglehart revived culture studies with The Silent Revolution (1977) on postmaterial values.

Political development and modernisation.

  • S.M. Lipset, "Some Social Requisites of Democracy" (1959): wealthier countries are more likely to be democratic.
  • Daniel Lerner, The Passing of Traditional Society (1958); W.W. Rostow, The Stages of Economic Growth (1960).
  • Samuel Huntington, Political Order in Changing Societies (1968): rapid change without strong institutions creates instability. Order matters more than regime type.

cards.h: Bringing history and the state back in
cards.b:
From the 1960s, historical and Marxist-influenced comparativists challenged modernisation theory.

  • Barrington Moore Jr., Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966): the routes to the modern world depend on how landlords, peasants and the bourgeoisie interact. "No bourgeois, no democracy."
  • Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979): revolutions in France, Russia and China arose from state breakdown under international pressure plus peasant revolt.
  • Bringing the State Back In (Evans, Rueschemeyer and Skocpol, eds., 1985): the state is an actor with its own interests, not just a reflection of society.
  • Dependency and world-system writers (Frank, Wallerstein, Cardoso) argued the national case cannot be understood without the international economy.

This is the historical-structural tradition. It focuses on a few big cases, long time spans, and "critical junctures" (also path dependence). Its weakness: few cases, so the findings are hard to generalise.

New institutionalism

James March and Johan Olsen, "The New Institutionalism" (1984), revived attention to institutions. Peter Hall and Rosemary Taylor (1996) separated three schools: historical (path dependence), rational choice (institutions as rules for strategic actors) and sociological (norms and cultural frames). Douglass North, Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance (1990), defined institutions as "the rules of the game".

Rational choice

Individuals pursue their interests. Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957): parties and voters act like firms and consumers. Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965): large groups struggle to organise. George Tsebelis, Veto Players (2002): policy change depends on how many actors can block it.

Critiques of rational choice: unrealistic assumptions; neglect of culture and history; "Green and Shapiro" (Pathologies of Rational Choice Theory, 1994) said it explains little.

Today scholars mix methods: comparative-historical analysis, statistics, case studies and experiments.

cards.h: India as a case in comparative politics
cards.b:
• The puzzle of Indian democracy. India became a democracy as a poor, diverse, mostly illiterate country, against Lipset's expectations. Lijphart, "The Puzzle of Indian Democracy: A Consociational Interpretation" (APSR, 1996), argued that power-sharing among groups (coalitions, federalism, minority rights) explains it.
  • Congress system. Rajni Kothari (1964) described a dominant-party system with competition inside the party. W.H. Morris-Jones saw "three idioms" of politics: modern, traditional and saintly.
  • State and society. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, The Modernity of Tradition (1967), argued that caste adapted to democracy. Atul Kohli and Pranab Bardhan studied the Indian state and its limits.
  • Federal comparison. India is compared with the US, Canada and Nigeria on federalism and with Brazil on development.
  • Post-colonial lens. Partha Chatterjee's "political society" and Mahmood Mamdani on the colonial state challenge Western categories.

India fits few single theories, which makes it a favourite "hard case".

Structure: define the field, with the aims and roots (Aristotle, Montesquieu). Explain the comparative method (Mill, Lijphart, most similar/most different). Present approaches in order, each with a thinker, a book and one critique: traditional, behavioural, systems, structural-functional, political culture, political development, historical-structural, institutionalism and rational choice. Add India as a case (Lijphart 1996).

A timeline table gives a neat, high-scoring finish.

quiz.q: Arend Lijphart's 1971 article named four methods. Which is NOT among them?
quiz.w: The four are experimental, statistical, comparative and case study.

quiz.q: The 'most similar systems' design is associated with:
quiz.w: The Logic of Comparative Social Inquiry (1970).

o: The New Revolution in Political Science

quiz.q: Which concept is NOT part of Almond's input functions?
quiz.w: Rule adjudication is an output function.

quiz.q: The Civic Culture (1963) identified which three political cultures?
quiz.w: Almond and Verba combined them into the 'civic culture'.

quiz.q: Samuel Huntington's Political Order in Changing Societies (1968) argues that:
o: Rapid modernisation without institutions causes instability
quiz.w: Political institutionalisation must keep pace with participation.

quiz.q: Who wrote Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966)?
quiz.w: Moore compared routes to the modern world.

quiz.q: The three new institutionalisms (Hall and Taylor, 1996) are:
Lijphart's 'The Puzzle of Indian Democracy' (1996) offers which explanation?
quiz.w: Power-sharing among groups helps explain democratic survival.

quiz.q: Anthony Downs's An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957) is a work of:
quiz.w: Parties and voters are modelled as rational maximisers.
